definition: Enfranchisement means the granting of a formal right or privilege, especially the right to vote.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word enfranchisement. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know enfranchisement should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: In 1920, the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment completed the enfranchisement of American women, millions of whom cast their first ballots that November.
Permission grants a small, revocable allowance for one activity, while enfranchisement confers a lasting formal right that belongs to the citizen.
Emancipation goes even further than enfranchisement, freeing a person from bondage or control entirely rather than granting one civic right.

Empowerment is the broad gaining of power, confidence, or standing, by any route — education, money, organizing. Enfranchisement is one precise legal event: the formal grant of a right, above all the vote. A community can feel empowered without winning any new right; enfranchisement puts the right on the books.

An authorization is official permission for one specific act — to access a file, to make one purchase — and it can expire or be revoked. Enfranchisement confers a lasting right that belongs to the citizen from then on. Authorization borrows power for a moment; enfranchisement grants it for good.

Naturalization is the formal grant of citizenship itself to someone born elsewhere, an entire legal status with many rights bundled inside. Enfranchisement is narrower: the grant of one civic right, especially the vote. Naturalization usually brings enfranchisement with it, but a group can be enfranchised without any citizenship changing.
Exclusion shuts a person out of participation — the condition enfranchisement is designed to end.
Suppression actively holds down a group's rights or voice rather than extending them.

For ninety years, the mining town of Coble Creek let only landowners vote on its schools, though miners' children filled every classroom.
The miners petitioned, lost, and petitioned again; they held rallies, published a weekly paper, and sent delegations to the state capitol.
None of that gave them what they were actually asking for, because confidence and organization are not the same thing as a right.
Then in 1954 the state legislature amended the town's charter, and the enfranchisement of every adult resident was finally written into law.
The next school-board election drew four times the usual turnout, and the first new budget rebuilt the crumbling east-side school within two years.
